title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
正統七年春二月歲當大比天下
之士就試于禮部者凡千人尚書
臣濙侍郎兼翰林院侍讀學士臣直
先期請官考試是月丁酉
上命臣英臣衷為考官同考則臣琛臣文
臣宏譽臣旋臣振臣員韞臣振臣舉
===
則臣鎰臣敬已亥
陛辭入院凡三試士中選者得百五
十人比舊額增其數焉猗歟盛哉
仰惟
皇上以至聖大德嗣承
列聖之統尊居寶位撫御萬方事
天以敬事

陛辭入院凡三試士中選者得百五
十人比舊額增其數焉猗歟盛哉
仰惟
皇上以至聖大德嗣承
列聖之統尊居寶位撫御萬方事
天以敬事
punctuated:
會試錄序

正統七年春二月，歲當大比，天下之士就試于禮部者凡千人。尚書臣濙、侍郎兼翰林院侍讀學士臣直先期請官考試。是月丁酉，上命臣英、臣衷為考官，同考則臣琛、臣文、臣宏、譽、臣旋、臣振、臣員、韞、臣振、臣舉、則、臣鎰、臣敬。已亥，陛辭入院。凡三試，士中選者得百五十人，比舊額增其數焉。猗歟盛哉！仰惟皇上以至聖大德，嗣承列聖之統，尊居寶位，撫御萬方，事天以敬，事
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the second month of spring in the seventh year of the Zhengtong era (1442), the year of the triennial examination, the scholars from throughout the empire who came to take the examination at the Ministry of Rites numbered roughly one thousand in all. Ahead of the scheduled date, the Minister of Rites, your servant [Hu] Ying 胡濙, and the Vice Minister concurrently serving as Hanlin Reader-in-Waiting Academician, your servant [Wang] Zhi 王直, petitioned for the appointment of officials to conduct the examination. On the dingyou day of that month, His Majesty appointed your servants [Wang] Ying 王英 and [Miao] Zhong 苗衷 as Examiners; as Associate Examiners, there were your servants Chen 琛, Wen 文, Hong 宏, Yu 譽, Xuan 旋, Zhen 振, Yuan 員, Yun 韞, Zhen 振, Ju 舉, Ze 則, Yi 鎰, and Jing 敬. On the jihai day, we took leave of the throne and entered the examination compound. After three sessions of testing in all, one hundred and fifty scholars were selected, an increase in number compared to the former quota. Oh, how splendid! Looking up, we reflect that the August Emperor, possessing supreme sageliness and great virtue, has succeeded to the line of the successive Sacred Emperors. Occupying in majesty the Precious Throne and soothing and governing the myriad regions, he serves Heaven with reverence, serves…

title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
親以誠務聖學以勤而愛民以仁心至
於命官必戒其盡職而選士則欲
得實才
聖心純一見於訓諭者盖惓惓也臣英
等承
命考較夙夜祗謹豈敢以虛文應
詔不求其實哉夫設科以取士也士
===
之力學明經者由此而進考其文
藝具有成法其命題也本於經史
其措詞也必根於實理今所較閱
務致其嚴差繆者黜之浮冗者斥
之深僻者抑之好奇以為工者去
之惟平易鬯達不失於理者取焉
夫豈過為去取之嚴哉盖惟恐取

等承
命考較夙夜祗謹豈敢以虛文應

===
之力學明經者由此而進考其文
藝具有成法其命題也本於經史
其措詞也必根於實理今所較閱
務致其嚴差繆者黜之浮冗者斥
之深僻者抑之好奇以為工者去
之惟平易舂達不失於理者取焉
夫豈過為去取之嚴哉蓋惟恐取
punctuated: 親以誠，務聖學以勤，而愛民以仁心。至於命官，必戒其盡職，而選士則欲得實才。聖心純一，見於訓諭者，盖惓惓也。臣英等承命考較，夙夜祗謹，豈敢以虛文應詔，不求其實哉！夫設科以取士也，士之力學明經者由此而進。考其文藝，具有成法：其命題也，本於經史；其措詞也，必根於實理。今所較閱，務致其嚴：差繆者黜之，浮冗者斥之，深僻者抑之，好奇以為工者去之，惟平易鬯達、不失於理者取焉。夫豈過為去取之嚴哉？盖惟恐取
translation_en: … his kin with sincerity, applies himself to sage learning with diligence, and loves the people with a benevolent heart. When appointing officials, he invariably admonishes them to fulfill their duties; and when selecting scholars, he desires to obtain genuine talent. His Sacred Mind is pure and unified, and what is manifested in his instructional edicts is truly earnest and unceasing. Having received the command to examine and evaluate the papers, your servant Ying and his colleagues have been reverent and cautious day and night; how could we dare respond to the imperial edict with empty words without seeking genuine substance? Now, the examinations are established to select scholars, and scholars who study diligently and master the Classics advance by this path. For examining their literary skill, there are established rules: the setting of questions is based on the Classics and Histories, and the phrasing of their answers must be rooted in substantive principle. In our present grading and review, we have striven to exercise the utmost strictness: those that were erroneous we eliminated, those that were superficial and verbose we rejected, those that were obscure and eccentric we suppressed, and those that indulged in novelty as a mark of craft we discarded; only those that were plain, fluent, and did not depart from principle did we select. How could this be an overly severe standard of acceptance and rejection? Indeed, our only fear was that in selecting…

title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
人無實不足以副
聖意也夫取人必以實行然必因言以
求其實士之與選者尤當發舒所
蘊對策
大廷由是第進士躋顯要行其所學
建功立名垂聲振耀斯著其實而
所謂文者非虛言矣宋歐陽修嘗
===
曰士方取其文詞類若浮而少實
及觀其臨事設施奮其事業隱然
為國名臣者不可勝數斯言盖誠
然也今豈無其人乎在士之自勉
何如耳英以譾才叨列侍從日近
清光恭聽
聖訓於命官取士恒諄諄然者謹識之

===
曰士方取其文詞類若浮而少實
及觀其臨事設施奮其事業隱然
爲國名臣者不可勝數斯言蓋誠
然也令豈無其人乎在士之自勉
何如耳〔英以謭才叨列侍從日近〕
清光恭聽
聖訓於命官取士恒諄諄然者謹識之
punctuated: 人無實，不足以副聖意也。夫取人必以實行，然必因言以求其實。士之與選者，尤當發舒所蘊，對策大廷，由是第進士，躋顯要，行其所學，建功立名，垂聲振耀，斯著其實，而所謂文者，非虛言矣。宋歐陽修嘗曰：「士方取其文詞，類若浮而少實；及觀其臨事設施，奮其事業，隱然為國名臣者，不可勝數。」斯言盖誠然也。今豈無其人乎？在士之自勉何如耳。英以譾才，叨列侍從，日近清光，恭聽聖訓，於命官取士恒諄諄然者，謹識之，
translation_en: … those selected might lack substance and thus fail to fulfill the Sacred Intention. Now, in selecting men, one must look to their actual conduct, yet one must rely on their words to seek out their substance. Those scholars who have been chosen ought especially to set forth the learning they have accumulated when replying to the policy questions in the Great Court; thereby they will be ranked as metropolitan graduates (jinshi), ascend to prominent and important posts, put into practice what they have learned, establish merit and reputation, and hand down a glorious name. In this way they will manifest their substance, and what is called their literary composition will not have been empty words. Ouyang Xiu 歐陽修 of the Song dynasty once said: "When scholars are first selected on the basis of their literary writings, they generally seem superficial and lacking in substance; yet when one observes them handling affairs and implementing measures, exerting themselves in their enterprises, those who stand out with quiet weight as renowned ministers of the state are beyond counting." These words are truly so. How could there be no such men today? It depends only on how the scholars exert themselves. With my meager talents, I, [Wang] Ying 王英, have been undeservedly ranked among the imperial attendants, daily drawing near to the pure radiance of the throne and reverently listening to the Sacred Instructions, which in appointing officials and selecting scholars have always been earnestly repeated; I have respectfully borne them in mind …

title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
不敢有忘故即其實書為小錄之
序以勸諸士子當務實效庶無負
於是選也
通議大夫禮部左侍郎兼翰林院
侍講學士王英謹序

侍講學士王〔英〕謹序
punctuated:
不敢有忘。故即其實，書為小錄之序，以勸諸士子當務實效，庶無負於是選也。
通議大夫、禮部左侍郎兼翰林院侍講學士王英謹序。
translation_en:
…and dare not forget them. Therefore, proceeding directly from the facts, I write this as the preface to the examination record, in order to exhort the scholars that they must devote themselves to practical efficacy, so that they may hopefully not fail to live up to this selection.

Respectfully prefaced by Wang Ying 王英, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Left Vice Minister of Rites, and concurrently Academician Expositor-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy.

title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
隱居以求其志行義以達其道
自誠明謂之性自明誠謂之教
易其田疇薄其稅斂民可使富也食之以
時用之以禮財不可勝用也
易
六二之動直以方也不習无不利地道光
也
===
大有柔得尊位大中而上下應之曰大有
其德剛健而文明應乎天而時行是
以元亨
君子安其身而後動易其心而後語定其
交而後求君子脩此三者故全也
昔者聖人之作易也幽賛於神明而生蓍
參天兩地而倚數

translation_en:
First Session

The Four Books:
"Living in retirement in order to pursue their aims; practicing righteousness in order to carry out their Way."
"Enlightenment resulting from sincerity is called nature; sincerity resulting from enlightenment is called instruction."
"Let them cultivate their fields well and make the taxes on them light, and the people may be made rich. Let them eat in accordance with the seasons and use resources in accordance with ritual propriety, and the wealth will be more than can be used."

Book of Changes (Yi):
"The movement of the second six is straight and thereby square. 'Without practice, there is nothing that is not advantageous': the Way of Earth is glorious."
"Possession in Great Measure (Dayou): the yielding obtains the honored position, great and central, and those above and below respond to it; hence it is called Possession in Great Measure. Its virtue is firm and strong, yet culturally brilliant; it responds to Heaven and acts in accordance with the times, and therefore there is supreme success."
"The noble man secures his person before he moves, composes his mind before he speaks, and settles his relationships before he makes requests. The noble man cultivates these three things, and therefore is complete."
"In ancient times, when the sages made the Changes, they mysteriously assisted the spiritual and luminous and produced the milfoil stalks; they assigned three to Heaven and two to Earth, and from this established the numbers."

Book of Documents (Shu):
"The Emperor said, 'Ah! Chief of the Four Mountains (Siyue), is there anyone who can direct my three rituals?' All said, 'Boyi 伯夷.' The Emperor…"

title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
曰俞咨伯汝作秩宗夙夜惟寅直哉
惟清
爾交脩予罔予棄予惟克邁乃訓說曰王
人求多聞時惟建事學于古訓乃有
獲
惟茲惟德稱用乂厥辟故一人有事于四
方若卜筮罔不是孚
申畫郊圻慎固封守以康四海
詩
===
二之日其同載纘武功言私其豵獻豜于
公
菁菁者莪在彼中陵既見君子錫我百朋
經始靈臺經之營之庶民攻之不日成之
經始勿亟庶民子來王在靈囿麀鹿
攸伏麀鹿濯濯白鳥翯翯王在靈沼
於牣魚躍
文王既勤止我應受之敷時繹思我徂維
求定

translation_en:
…generations. Among later rulers of All under Heaven, words exhorting and encouraging ministers and subjects have never been lacking, yet none have matched the flourishing excellence of our Dynasty. The Grand Pronouncements (Da gao) imperially composed by Grand Progenitor Emperor Gao (Taizu, the Hongwu Emperor), and The Unseen Rewards of Doing Good (Wei shan yin zhi) and True Examples of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi) by Grand Ancestor Emperor Wen (Taizong, the Yongle Emperor)—the creation of these three books follows the very same principle as the instructions and announcements in the Classics. Among them are passages that speak of "maintaining the mind and upholding integrity," of "spreading virtue and bestowing kindness," and of "as the constant norm of Heaven and the principle of Earth, nothing is more revered than one's parents." Great indeed are the sage words! Truly, they intend that the people of the world, in reading them, will be inspired to rise up and follow their instructions, thereby fulfilling the Way of cultivating the self, doing good, being loyal to the ruler, and being filial to parents. Yet if one is to embody them and practice them throughout one's whole life, what should be taken as the essential point? This is what ought to be clearly expounded; answer with your whole mind.

Question: The Way originates from Heaven. When the sages composed the Classics, the Way resided in the sages, and the Classics became that wherein the Way is lodged. Can the intent behind their composition of the Classics be traced to its origin and stated? When Master Shao [Shao Yong 邵雍] discussed the Way of Heaven, he invariably spoke of it in terms of the Classics, saying, "The sages modeled themselves on Heaven through the Classics; Heaven has four storehouses, and the sages likewise have four storehouses." Why is this? The Way of Heaven is to give birth to, nurture, and bring to maturity the myriad things; the composition of the Classics is to illuminate the Way of emperors and kings. How then can this be called modeling on Heaven? Moreover, as for "storehouse,"…

之義何所取？蓋必有至論也。性理之書，頒于四方乆矣，學者豈不熟讀而玩味焉？言之毋畧。
問：《周書》曰：「舉能其官，惟爾之能。」孔子曰：「舉爾所知。」蓋舉賢，人臣之所當先也。古之所舉，有不棄讎、不避親者；有舉公正聰明、經術精通、善聽獄訟與夫練習法令者；又有以學問該博、行實純固而舉之者；有教子登壇、韜畧世授，父舉其子，勳業無愧者；又有舉同巷不求見、無書抵政府者。此皆舉之至公也。其舉者與其所舉之人及其政績，可悉言之歟？今朝廷屢詔大臣各舉其所知，繆舉者有同坐之令，求才可謂嚴矣，而所舉未盡得人，何歟？伊欲所舉盡如古人之可稱者，必有其道，宜詳言之。

translation_en:
… meaning of “storehouse” (fu) derived? Surely there must be a definitive explanation. Books on nature and principle (xingli) have long been promulgated throughout the four quarters of the empire; how could scholars not have read them thoroughly and savored their meaning? Speak of this without omission.

Question: The Book of Zhou states: “Recommend those who are capable of their offices, and this will prove your own capability.” Confucius said: “Recommend those whom you know.” Indeed, recommending the worthy is what a minister ought to put first. Among those recommended in antiquity, there were cases where one did not reject an enemy or avoid a relative; there were cases of recommending those who were fair, upright, and perceptive, thoroughly versed in classical scholarship, skilled at hearing lawsuits, and practiced in laws and ordinances; there were also cases of recommending men for their broad learning and pure, steadfast conduct; there were cases where a father instructed his son to ascend the general's platform, handing down military strategy through the generations, and when the father recommended his own son, the son's meritorious achievements brought no shame; and there were also cases of recommending someone who lived in the same lane yet never sought an audience, and who sent no letters to the seat of government. All of these were instances of supreme impartiality in recommendation. Can you recount in full those who made these recommendations, the persons they recommended, and their administrative achievements? Now the Imperial Court has repeatedly decreed that grand ministers should each recommend those whom they know, and there is an ordinance of joint liability for making erroneous recommendations. The search for talent may well be called strict, yet those recommended are not all the right men—why is this? If we wish that those recommended should all be as praiseworthy as the men of antiquity, there must be a way to achieve this. Expound upon it in detail.

Question: The employment of military commanders has been valued since antiquity, yet there must first be a way to recruit them before they can be employed. In the Han dynasty, they either recruited sons of good families from the Six Commanduries, or took men from the Three Rivers (Sanhe) …

試武藝可得而詳歟宋武學嘗廢有上
書力言當興之者且薦知兵法者為師
===
又誰歟或謂胡翼之嘗有所陳其言果
行之歟當天下承平四方無虞武不可
弛將須得人惟養之於武學取之於武
舉歟抑亦取蘇范舉試之言庶可以得
其人歟其備言以觀平日所學
問自宋以來學者之師必稱安定先生而
當時則又以孫泰山石徂徠可以並□
也安定之在湖學以聖人體用之學
教出其門者多大才為名臣然論□
punctuated:
立功自小校至将帥者，可數之歟？唐、宋皆置武舉科，其置之所始、舉之之目及所舉之人，亦可數之歟？或以李廣、趙充國、郭子儀、高志寧、令狐挺之属是已。數人者之功業何如？其人盖未止此也。武舉之外，又有武學以教将臣子弟。其始建議與判學事者誰歟？學之教法及所試武藝可得而詳歟？宋武學嘗廢，有上書力言當興之者，且薦知兵法者為師，又誰歟？或謂胡翼之嘗有所陳，其言果行之歟？當天下承平、四方無虞，武不可弛，将須得人，惟養之於武學、取之於武舉歟？抑亦取蘇、范舉試之言，庶可以得其人歟？其備言以觀平日所學。

translation_en:
…who achieved merit and rose from junior officer to commander-in-chief—can they be enumerated? Both the Tang and the Song instituted the Military Examination (wuju) category; can the origins of its establishment, the subjects of its examinations, and the men selected through it also be enumerated? Some point to men such as Li Guang 李廣, Zhao Chongguo 趙充國, Guo Ziyi 郭子儀, Gao Zhining 高志寧, and Linghu Ting 令狐挺 as examples. What were the meritorious achievements of these several men? Surely such men were not limited to these alone. Beyond the Military Examinations, there were also Military Schools (wuxue) to instruct the sons and younger brothers of military commanders and officials. Who was it that first proposed their establishment and served as Supervisor of the School (pan xueshi)? Can the instructional methods of the schools and the military arts tested therein be set forth in detail? In the Song, the Military School was once abolished; who again was it that submitted a memorial forcefully arguing that it ought to be revived, and furthermore recommended someone well-versed in military strategy to serve as instructor? Some say that Hu Yizhi 胡翼之 [Hu Yuan 胡瑗] once presented a proposal on this matter; were his words actually put into practice? At a time when the realm enjoys enduring peace and the four quarters are free from alarm, military preparedness must not be relaxed and we must obtain the right men for commanders. Should we solely nurture them in Military Schools and select them through Military Examinations, or should we also adopt the proposals of Su [Shi 蘇軾] and Fan [Zhongyan 范仲淹] regarding recommendation and testing, so that we may perhaps obtain the right men? Expound upon this fully so that we may observe what you have studied in your daily life.

Question: Since the Song dynasty, in speaking of teachers of scholars, one invariably praises Master Anding 安定先生 [Hu Yuan 胡瑗], while in his own day Sun Taishan 孫泰山 [Sun Fu 孫復] and Shi Culai 石徂徠 [Shi Jie 石介] were also considered worthy of being named alongside him. When Anding was at the Huzhou Prefectural School (Huxue), he taught on the basis of the sages' [learning of] substance and function (ti yong) [?]; those who came from his gate included many men of great talent who became renowned officials. Yet as for what they [divided into substance and]…

title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
用者何所分為名臣者何人及入教國
子天下之士尊師之而或謂其所教乃
科舉進取之業非義理之學而論者又
以從其游者有道學之大儒有節操之
君子非科舉之學也其所謂大儒君子
者抑知其人歟若泰山徂徠亦儒者也
其出處學行亦豈無可稱者歟悉為陳
之

punctuated: 用者，何所分？為名臣者，何人？及入教國子，天下之士尊師之。而或謂其所教，乃科舉進取之業，非義理之學；而論者又以從其游者，有道學之大儒，有節操之君子，非科舉之學也。其所謂大儒、君子者，抑知其人歟？若泰山、徂徠，亦儒者也，其出處、學行，亦豈無可稱者歟？悉為陳之。
translation_en: … [substance and] function—how were they divided? And who were those who became renowned officials? When he subsequently entered [the capital] to instruct the Sons of State (students at the Directorate of Education), scholars throughout the realm revered him as their teacher. Yet some claimed that what he taught was merely the business of advancing through the civil service examinations, rather than the learning of moral principle; whereas other commentators held that among those who studied under him there were great Confucians of the Learning of the Way (Daoxue) and gentlemen of moral integrity, so that it was not mere examination learning. As for those whom they called great Confucians and gentlemen, do you know who these men were? And as for Taishan (Sun Fu 孫復) and Culai (Shi Jie 石介), they too were Confucian scholars; how could their careers in and out of office, their scholarship, and their conduct be without anything worthy of praise? Set forth all of this in full.

君子之處也，守其道；而其出也，行其道。蓋處之所守，即其所達之道；用之所行，即其所求之志。君子之出處雖有不同，而其道亦豈有異哉？夫謂之隱居者，潛而未用，無官守言責也，其將何所守哉？亦曰「求其志」而已。求其志者，守其所達之道也。道莫大於仁，念慮之間惟仁是求，而一毫之非仁不敢存也；道不外乎義，起居之際惟義是守，而一毫之非義不敢由也。所守如是，則達而可行之道已備於己矣。謂之行義者，出而致用，有名位職守也，又將何所為哉？亦曰「達其道」而已。達其道者，行其所求之志也。蓋仁則吾志之

Four Books

"Living in retirement in order to pursue one's aspirations; practicing righteousness in order to carry out one's Way." [Analects 16.11]

Yao Kui 姚夔

Comment by Associate Examiner and Expositor-in-Waiting Liu 劉: On this topic, most writers erred by being overly diffuse; only this essay is concise and clear without losing the original meaning of pursuing one's aspirations and carrying out one's Way, so I have singled it out for publication.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Miao 苗: This essay is concise in wording and complete in meaning, so I have selected it.
Comment by Examiner and Vice Minister Wang 王: Balanced and sound, worthy of selection.

When the gentleman remains in retirement, he holds fast to his Way; when he goes forth into public life, he practices his Way. For what he holds fast to in retirement is the very Way he carries out, and what he practices when employed is the very aspiration he has pursued. Although the gentleman's going forth and remaining in retirement differ, how could his Way be any different? Now, what is called "living in retirement" means living in obscurity and not yet being employed, having neither official charge nor responsibility to speak out. To what, then, shall he hold fast? It is simply called "pursuing his aspirations." To pursue his aspirations is to hold fast to the Way that he will carry out. Nothing in the Way is greater than benevolence; in his thoughts and reflections he seeks only benevolence, not daring to harbor the slightest bit of what is not benevolent. The Way is nothing outside of righteousness; in his daily conduct and movements he holds fast only to righteousness, not daring to follow the slightest bit of what is not righteous. Holding fast in this manner, the Way that can be carried out and practiced when he achieves prominence is already complete within himself. What is called "practicing righteousness" means going forth to be put to use, having rank, position, and official duties. What, then, shall he do? It is simply called "carrying out his Way." To carry out his Way is to practice the aspirations he has pursued. For benevolence is what my aspirations…

translation_en:
…abides; now, when one presides over governance and showers its enriching favors upon the people, nothing is not the dispensation of this benevolence. Righteousness, too, is that which my resolve upholds; now, when one manifests it in practical affairs and makes illustrious one's meritorious achievements in the state, nothing is not the expression of this righteousness. Is this not the gentleman upholding his Way when in retirement, and practicing his Way when in office? Moreover, as for this saying, it existed in antiquity; Confucius recited it and again sighed that he had not yet seen such a person. Former Confucians, however, held that only the likes of Yi Yin 伊尹 and Taigong 太公 were worthy of matching it. Indeed, Yi Yin and Taigong emerged from plowing the fields of Youxin 莘 and fishing by the Wei 渭 River to assist in completing the kingly enterprises of the Shang and Zhou dynasties—as for what is called "pursuing one's resolve" and "realizing one's Way," is it not truly so? Scholars of later ages who aspire to be employed in office ought to begin from living in retirement to pursue their resolve.

"Have them cultivate their fields well, and make their taxes and levies light, so the people may be made rich; have them consume according to the seasons, and spend according to the rites, so their wealth will be more than can be used." [Mencius 7A.23]
Liu Yan 劉儼

For attending to the fundamental is the means to enrich the source of their wealth, and practicing frugality is the means to check the outflow of their wealth;…

養民之政，孰有加於此哉？昔者孟子之論王政，着曰：民者，國之本；財者，民之命。欲養其民者，必也制其田里，教之樹藝，使無不耕之田；征取什一，惟正之供，使無厚斂之擾。則民有恒産，而得遂仰事俯育之樂、飽食暖衣之願，民其有不富乎？夫民既務本以遂其生，將必有侈用傷財之失。又必使食之以時，而不時而食之有其禁；用之以禮，而踰禮過用之有其法。則用度有節，所積者陳陳而相因，所取者源源而不竭，財其可勝用乎？故曰：大賢論養民之政，教之務本而節儉，則民富而用足者，此也。大抵禮義生於富足，民無恒産則無恒心。是以孟子之論王政，拳拳以養民為先務，惜乎託之空言而已。吁！孟子之言雖不見用於當時，而實可法於萬世也。

translation_en:
… In governance that nourishes the people, what could surpass this? In former times, when Mencius discussed kingly governance, he meant [?] to say: The people are the foundation of the state, and wealth is the lifeblood of the people. One who wishes to nourish his people must regulate their fields and homesteads and teach them arboriculture and agriculture, so that there are no unplowed fields; and he must levy a tithe of one-tenth as the sole regular tax contribution, so that there is no harassment from heavy exactions. Then the people will have constant livelihoods and be able to fulfill the joy of serving their parents above and nurturing their wives and children below, as well as their desire for full bellies and warm clothes—how could the people not be wealthy? Now, once the people attend to the fundamental occupation in order to fulfill their livelihoods, there will inevitably be the failing of extravagant expenditure harming their wealth. One must further ensure that they consume things according to the season, with prohibitions against consuming them out of season; and that they use things in accordance with ritual propriety, with laws against transgressing ritual and excessive expenditure. Then expenditures will be regulated, what is stored up will accumulate layer upon layer, and what is drawn upon will flow continuously without exhaustion—how could their wealth ever be fully used up? Therefore it is said: When the great worthy discussed governance that nourishes the people, he taught them to attend to the fundamental and practice frugality, so that the people would be wealthy and resources sufficient—this is what is meant. Generally speaking, ritual propriety and righteousness arise from abundance, and if the people lack constant livelihoods, they will lack constant minds. For this reason, when Mencius discussed kingly governance, he earnestly took nourishing the people as the first priority; alas, it was merely entrusted to empty words! Ah! Although Mencius's words were not put to use in his own time, they can truly serve as a model for ten thousand generations.

Book of Changes (Yi)

"The movement of the Six in the Second place is straight and therefore square. 'Without rehearsal, nothing is unfavorable': the Way of Earth is glorious."

一爻居中得正獨得坤道之純故前聖繫其辭後聖
punctuated:
題真而行文順，佳作也。
考試官學士苗批：詞簡理明，得潔淨法定旨。
考試官侍郎王批：典實不浮，視他卷爲優。
惟坤之德無不純，故坤之功無不著。盖柔順中正者，坤德之純也；自然光顯者，功用之著也。惟其備坤德之純，故必著自然之功，此吾夫子釋《坤》六二之爻義也。今夫《坤》之六二，以柔居柔，處中得正。周公繫爻既曰「直方大，不習无不利」，吾夫子《象傳》復釋之以此，何哉？誠以《坤》之六二柔順正固，則德之體無不備；賦形有定，則德之用無不全。故其承天而動也，直則生物而不屈撓，方則賦形而不移易。然惟其有是直方之德，故不繩而自直，不矩而自方，固不待於學習而自無不利也。其所以自無不利者，乃地道光也。謂之地道之光，則生物之功光輝宣著，自有不可得而掩矣。故曰「惟坤之德無不純，故坤之功無不著」者，此也。抑考《坤》六爻，初之履、上之極，不足言矣；三、五以陰居陽而不正，四處上卦之下而不中，皆非坤道之純也。惟六二一爻，居中得正，獨得坤道之純，故前聖繫其辭，後聖

… [grasps] the topic truly and the writing flows smoothly; it is an excellent piece.
Examiner and Academician Miao (Miao衷) comments: The wording is concise and the reasoning clear; it captures the definitive purport of the pure and refined method [of the Classic of Changes].
Examiner and Vice Minister Wang (Wang 英) comments: Allusive and substantial without being superficial; compared to other papers, it is superior.

Because the virtue of Kun (the Receptive) is utterly pure, the achievement of Kun is utterly manifest. For being yielding, compliant, central, and correct is the purity of Kun's virtue; being naturally glorious and illustrious is the manifestation of its functional achievement. Because it possesses the purity of Kun's virtue in full, it necessarily manifests a natural achievement—this is our Master [Confucius] explaining the meaning of the six in the second place line of the hexagram Kun. Now, in the six in the second place of Kun, a yielding line occupies a yielding position, dwelling in the center and attaining correctness. After the Duke of Zhou appended the line text saying, "Straight, square, great; without repeated practice, there is nothing that is not advantageous," why did our Master in the Commentary on the Images (Xiangzhuan) further explain it in these words? Truly it is because the six in the second place of Kun is yielding, compliant, correct, and firm, so that the substance of its virtue is completely provided; and in bestowing forms it has regularity, so that the function of its virtue is completely whole. Therefore, when it responds to Heaven and moves: being straight, it generates things without bending or flinching; being square, it bestows forms without shifting or altering. Yet precisely because it possesses this virtue of straightness and squareness, it is straight of itself without a plumb line, and square of itself without a carpenter's square; indeed, without waiting upon learning and practice, there is naturally nothing in which it is not advantageous. The reason why there is naturally nothing in which it is not advantageous is that the Way of Earth is glorious. Calling it the glory of the Way of Earth means that the achievement of generating things shines forth and is brilliantly displayed, such that it naturally cannot be concealed. Therefore, when I say "Because the virtue of Kun is utterly pure, the achievement of Kun is utterly manifest," this is what is meant. Moreover, if we examine the six lines of Kun: the treading frost of the first line and the extreme position of the top line need not even be mentioned; the third and fifth lines occupy yang positions with yin lines and so are not correct, while the fourth line dwells at the bottom of the upper trigram and so is not central—none of these represents the purity of the Way of Kun. Only the single line of the six in the second place dwells in the center and attains correctness, alone obtaining the purity of the Way of Kun. Therefore, the former sage [the Duke of Zhou] appended its words, and the later sage [Confucius]…

人能致謹於言行交接之際，則自脩之道備矣。盖動與語者，言行之慎於己也；定交者，己之接於人也。苟能於此三者無一而不致其謹，則自脩之道盡而君子之德全矣。今夫身者，吾之身也。身有不安，則動必有失；君子必先安其身而後動，則動不妄動，而動惟厥時矣。心者，吾之神明。心有不平，則發言必躁；君子必先易其心而後言，則言不妄發，而發必當理矣。至若通彼此之情，非所謂交乎？若交無所定，則求必無益；君子必先定其交而後求，則求不徒求，而求則有

"The superior man composes his person before he moves; he calms his mind before he speaks; he establishes his relations before he makes requests. By cultivating these three things, the superior man achieves completeness."

Bai Gui 白圭

When a person can exercise utmost caution in speech, action, and intercourse with others, the way of self-cultivation is complete. For moving and speaking concern the prudence of one's own words and deeds, whereas establishing relations concerns how one interacts with others. If in all three of these one never fails to exercise the utmost caution, then the way of self-cultivation is fulfilled and the virtue of the superior man is made whole. Now, the person is one's own self. If one's person is not composed, one's actions will surely go astray; the superior man must first compose his person before he moves, so that he does not move recklessly, and moves only at the proper time. The mind is one's spiritual intelligence. If the mind is not calm, one's speech will surely be rash; the superior man must first calm his mind before he speaks, so that his words are not uttered recklessly, and when uttered, surely accord with principle. As for communicating feelings between oneself and others, is this not what is meant by relations? If relations are not firmly established, making a request will surely be of no avail; the superior man must first establish his relations before he makes a request, so that he does not ask in vain, and when he asks, there is…

… beneficial to oneself. Composing one's person before acting, calming one's mind before speaking, and establishing one's relationships before making requests—all of these are essentials for cultivating oneself. If the superior man fails to cultivate not a single one of these three, how then could the Way of the superior man be anything less than complete? Furthermore, if we examine the "Top Nine" line of the hexagram Yi [Increase], one seeks benefit from others and gains nothing, and on the contrary there are those who attack him. The Sage elaborated on it in these words because he wished for people to exhaust the goodness of the Way of Increase. He also said: "If one acts while in precariousness, the people will not join him; if one speaks while in fear, the people will not respond to him; if one makes requests without having established a relationship, the people will not grant them to him. When none join or grant anything to him, those who would injure him arrive." This was meant to warn people against the error of exclusively seeking to benefit oneself; this too must not go unexamined.

translation_en:
When the sage ruler sought an official to take charge of the rites and obtained unanimous agreement from public opinion, he further approved the recommendation of the assembled ministers and instructed the appointee in the way of serving the spirits. For in the way of serving the spirits, nothing is greater than reverence. When the sage ruler sought an official to take charge of the rites and found the right man, how could he not instruct him in the reverence required for serving the spirits?

In antiquity, when Emperor Shun consulted the Four Peaks, his meaning was as if to say: In ritual, nothing is more important than sacrifice. Sacrificing to the heavenly spirits, offering to the earthly deities, and presenting offerings to human ghosts—these three are the greatest of the rites. An official must be appointed to take charge of these affairs, and you, the Four Peaks, must recommend a worthy man to be employed. Thereupon, the Four Peaks, together with the feudal lords present at court, jointly recommended Boyi 伯夷. For Boyi's worthiness was known not only to the Four Peaks, but was known to all the ministers alike; it was known not only to all the ministers alike, but Emperor Shun knew it as well. Therefore, following their recommendation, Shun immediately approved of it and commanded him to serve as Director of Sacrifices (Zhizong 秩宗). The Director of Sacrifices is the official who arranges the order of the hundred spirits, taking the ancestral temple as the chief concern.

"You, Boyi, occupying the office of Director of Sacrifices—how should you conduct yourself? Only with reverence, and nothing more. In the morning maintain this reverence, and do not alter by evening; in the evening maintain this reverence, and do not grow lax by morning. If you are capable of reverence, your mind will be free from crooked selfishness and will be upright; being upright, your mind will remain ever pure and clear, untainted by material desires. Both purity and uprightness are attained through reverence. If you can act thus, you will be able to move and reach the divine spirits, and you will have nothing to be ashamed of in your office as Director of Sacrifices."

Furthermore, if we observe Emperor Shun's appointment of the Nine Officials: when Great Yu 大禹 was made Minister of Works (Sikong 司空), he said, "Exert yourself!"; when consulting Chui 垂 and consulting Yi 益, he said, "Go, and be harmonious in your duties!" Yet when he came to appointing Boyi, he uniquely instructed him with the words, "Morning and night, be reverent"; and when Boyi yielded in favor of Kui 夔 and Long 龍, he again instructed him, saying, "Go, be欽 (reverent)!" From beginning to end he spoke in terms of reverence, because sacrificial rites must take reverence as their foundation. That the sage Emperor Shun exercised such utmost care regarding the rites…

A worthy ruler relies on his minister to assist his virtue and takes upon himself the effort of strenuous practice; when a great minister offers counsel to his ruler, he must expound upon the way of learning. For among the duties of a minister, none takes precedence over assisting the ruler's virtue, and in the way of a ruler, nothing is more important than advancing in learning. Since the worthy ruler already relies on his minister to assist his virtue, how could the great minister not counsel him in the way of learning? In antiquity, when Gaozong 高宗 charged Fu Yue 傅說, he spoke to this effect: "You occupy the office of chief minister, in which nothing takes precedence over assisting my virtue. You must temper hardness with softness, just as malt and yeast combine to achieve their effect; you must temper the unacceptable with the acceptable, just as salt and plum combine to achieve their flavor. Do not abandon me and fail to exhaust your heart, nor forsake me and fail to fulfill your duty. title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
之於踐履力行爾之訓者若此汝說不言可乎說
也聞高宗之言特稱王以告之謂夫人非生而知之
莫不求聞於人必也廣詢眾論博采群言使無一善
之或遺則可以經綸大經建立大本而措諸事業矣
然資於人者固足以立事苟不反求諸巳則無以明
其理是故堯舜典謨之言乃古訓也必學以領會之
禹湯誓誥之辭亦古訓也必學以融貫之則理之在
於古者即吾心之所得而理之在吾心者即古訓之
所在則向之所聞於人者非徒聞矣又何事之不可
===
建而功之不可成哉傅說推言爲學之道至此可謂
善於輔君而無負於高宗之所望矣抑觀高宗之得
傅說置諸相位求誨之心盖拳拳焉而說也進戒之
辭屢矣前篇有曰知之非艱行之惟艱所以責其躬
行之實將進爲學之說此則因克邁乃訓之命而告
以此其開萬世論學之源實自此始

之於踐履。力行爾之訓者若此，汝說不言可乎？說也聞高宗之言，特稱王以告之，謂夫人非生而知之，莫不求聞於人，必也廣詢眾論、博采群言，使無一善之或遺，則可以經綸大經、建立大本，而措諸事業矣。然資於人者固足以立事，苟不反求諸巳，則無以明其理。是故堯、舜典謨之言，乃古訓也，必學以領會之；禹、湯誓誥之辭，亦古訓也，必學以融貫之。則理之在於古者即吾心之所得，而理之在吾心者即古訓之所在，則向之所聞於人者非徒聞矣，又何事之不可建、而功之不可成哉？傅說推言爲學之道至此，可謂善於輔君，而無負於高宗之所望矣。抑觀高宗之得傅說，置諸相位，求誨之心盖拳拳焉，而說也進戒之辭屢矣。前篇有曰：「知之非艱，行之惟艱。」所以責其躬行之實。將進爲學之說，此則因「克邁乃訓」之命而告以此，其開萬世論學之源，實自此始。

詩
經始靈臺，經之營之。庶民攻之，不日成之。經始勿亟，庶民子來。王在靈囿，麀鹿攸伏。麀鹿濯濯，白
translation_en:
…put into actual practice. Since I shall exert myself to carry out your instructions like this, how can you, Yue, remain silent?" Hearing Gaozong's words, Fu Yue specifically addressed him as "King" to advise him, saying that since no man is born with knowledge, everyone must seek to learn by hearing from others. One must inquire widely into public opinion and gather words broadly from the multitude so that not a single good point is overlooked; then one can order the great norms, establish the great foundation, and put them into practice in one's undertakings. Yet while drawing upon others is indeed sufficient to accomplish tasks, if one does not also seek within oneself, there is no way to illuminate the underlying principles. Therefore, the words of the canons and counsels of Yao and Shun are ancient lessons, and one must study to comprehend them; the words of the oaths and announcements of Yu and Tang are likewise ancient lessons, and one must study to thoroughly master them. Then the principles that existed in antiquity become what is attained in one's own mind, and the principles in one's own mind become where the ancient lessons reside. Thus what was previously heard from others is no longer merely heard—and what undertaking could not be established, what achievement could not be brought to completion? In extending his discourse on the way of learning to this point, Fu Yue may truly be called skillful at assisting his lord and worthy of what Gaozong hoped for in him. Moreover, when we observe how Gaozong, having obtained Fu Yue and placed him in the office of chief councillor, was so earnestly devoted in his desire for instruction, we see too that Yue repeatedly presented words of admonition. In the preceding chapter it is said, "To know is not difficult; to act is what is difficult," by which he urged upon the king the reality of personal practice. When he was about to present his teaching on learning here, it was prompted by the king's charge that "I can energetically carry out your instructions" that he advised him thus. Indeed, the opening of the fountainhead of discussions on learning for ten thousand generations truly began from this.

Book of Odes (Shijing)
"When he began to measure out the Numinous Terrace, he measured it and planned it. The common people worked at it, and in less than a day completed it. When he began to measure it out, he said, 'Do not hurry,' yet the common people came like sons. The king was in the Numinous Park, where the does were lying down. The does were sleek and shining, the white…"

同考試官知縣陳批：融會民樂之意，文辭瑩澤，洗去陳言，盖深於葩經者也。
同考試官脩撰林批：以民樂本於文王德化，詞語舂容，寫出當時民樂氣象，佳作也。
考試官學士苗批：形容文王德化及民之深，故民樂而物遂其性，善言詩者矣。

聖人有所為而民樂成其功，聖人随所寓而物各遂其性。盖民樂成其功，則文王德之所感者深；物各遂其性，則文王德之所及者廣矣。詩人形諸詠歌，厥有旨哉！夫國之有臺，所以望氛祲、察災祥、時觀游、節勞佚也。謂之靈者，言其倏然而成，如神靈之所為也。文王是臺之作，方其經之以度其地，營之以表其位，斯時也，若未假於用民力，而来攻之民已至，同心以趨事，協力以赴工，故不待曠日之久，而成於不日之頃。雖文王心恐煩民，戒令勿亟，而民皆懽忻踴躍，如子
translation_en:
… the white birds were glistening and sleek. The King was in the Spirit Pond; oh, how full it was of leaping fish!”

Luo Min 駱敏

Associate Examiner District Magistrate Chen 陳 comments: He thoroughly grasps the meaning of the people's joy. His diction is lustrous and polished, sweeping away clichés; he is truly someone deeply versed in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing).
Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Lin 林 comments: He grounds the people's joy in the moral transformation wrought by King Wen. The phrasing is unhurried and dignified, capturing the atmosphere of popular joy at that time. A fine piece!
Examiner Academician Miao 苗 comments: He describes how deeply King Wen's moral transformation reached the people, so that the people rejoiced and creatures fulfilled their natures. He is truly adept at expounding the Odes!
Examiner Vice Minister Wang 王 comments: This composition captures the intent of the poet in singing the praises of King Wen.

When the sage undertakes a work, the people gladly bring his achievement to completion; wherever the sage happens to dwell, all creatures fulfill their respective natures. Indeed, that the people gladly brought his achievement to completion shows how deeply King Wen's virtue moved them; that all creatures fulfilled their respective natures shows how broadly King Wen's virtue extended. When the poet gave expression to this in song, how purposeful it was! Now, the reason a state has a terrace is to observe atmospheric omens, examine signs of calamity and auspice, provide for seasonal sightseeing and recreation, and regulate toil and ease. Calling it "Spirit" (Ling 靈) means that it was completed suddenly, as if made by divine spirits. In constructing this terrace, just as King Wen was measuring it to survey the ground and laying it out to mark its positions—at that very moment, as if before he had even resorted to conscripting the people's labor—the people coming to build it had already arrived, hastening to the task with one heart and joining in the work with united strength. Thus, without waiting for a long stretch of time, it was completed in the span of just a few days. Although King Wen, fearing in his heart to trouble the people, cautioned and ordered them not to hurry, the people all rejoiced and leaped with eagerness, like sons…

之趨父事，不召而自來矣。其得民心之樂爲何如哉！靈囿者，臺下之囿，所以域養鳥獸者也；靈沼者，囿中之沼，所以蕃育魚鱉者也。文王之在靈囿，見其鹿之牝者，則安而不擾，濯濯然而肥澤；鳥之白者，則翯翯然而潔白：此飛走者樂其爲飛走也。文王之在靈沼，見其魚滿而躍，洋洋然而得其所：此鱗介者樂其爲鱗介也。物之遂其性者又何如哉！噫！因所爲而樂其功之成，因所寓而樂其物之盛，非文王之德感民之深，曷克以致此歟？是詩四章，皆述民樂之詞：此二章樂文王有臺池鳥獸之樂，後二章樂文王有辟雝鐘鼓之樂。孟子曰：「古之人與民偕樂，故能樂也。」讀是詩，可以想見文王之德化矣。

文王旣勤止，我應受之。敷時繹思，我徂維求定。
翁世資

同考試官脩撰林批：形容繹思求定之意，詞語
translation_en:
…hastening to their father's affairs, coming of their own accord without being summoned. How great was the joy with which he won the hearts of the people! The Marvelous Park (Lingyou) was the park beneath the terrace, used as an enclosure for raising birds and beasts; the Marvelous Pond (Lingzhao) was the pond within the park, used for breeding fish and turtles. When King Wen was in the Marvelous Park, he saw that the does were tranquil and undisturbed, sleek and plump, and that the white birds were gleaming and pure white—thus creatures that fly and run rejoiced in their flying and running. When King Wen was at the Marvelous Pond, he saw it full of leaping fish, swimming about contentedly in their element—thus creatures with scales and shells rejoiced in their scales and shells. How great, too, was the way all creatures fulfilled their natural tendencies! Alas! Because of what he built, the people rejoiced in the completion of his work; because of where he dwelt, they rejoiced in the abundance of his creatures. Had King Wen's virtue not moved the people so deeply, how could this have been brought about? All four stanzas of this ode express the joy of the people: these first two stanzas rejoice that King Wen had the pleasures of his terrace, pond, birds, and beasts, while the latter two stanzas rejoice that King Wen had the pleasures of the Hall of State (Biyong) and its bells and drums. Mencius said, "The ancients shared their pleasures with the people, and therefore they were able to enjoy them." Reading this ode, one can envision the transforming virtue of King Wen.

"King Wen labored earnestly; it is right that we have received [his inheritance]. We shall spread abroad this ever-cherished thought, and go forth only to seek stability."
By Weng Shizi 翁世資.

title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
諄切足以感動人心深得詩人之旨佳作也
考試官學士苗批講貫透徹頌義德而告成功之意
藹然見於言表矣
考試官侍郎王批詞婉而意足者此卷得之
前王之大業既當受之於己前王之功德尤當布之
以安民也夫創業者前聖之功而圖治者後王之責今
武王承文王之業苟不推其功德以賚有功將何以
求天下之安定哉是詩頌文武之功而言其大封功
臣之意若曰維我文王不遑暇食而咸和萬民望道
===
未見而撫有方夏其勤勞天下可謂至矣今我後人
受而有之纘三分有二之鴻業承四方攸同之丕緒
其何敢以自專而不思所以往求天下之安哉於是
合吾分封之臣而進之於文王之廟敷其德之在人
而可懷思者以賚爾在位之諸侯布其功之在人而
可慨念者以封爾有功之臣子夫豈有他哉盖欲諸
臣各以文王之心爲心而於斯民之未安者思有以
安之也皆以文王之德爲德而於天下之未定者思
有以定之也如是則可以副我求定之心而無愧於

前王之大業，既當受之於己；前王之功德，尤當布之以安民也。夫創業者，前聖之功；而圖治者，後王之責。今武王承文王之業，苟不推其功德以賚有功，將何以求天下之安定哉？是詩頌文、武之功，而言其大封功臣之意，若曰：維我文王，不遑暇食而咸和萬民，望道未見而撫有方夏，其勤勞天下可謂至矣。今我後人受而有之，纘三分有二之鴻業，承四方攸同之丕緒，其何敢以自專，而不思所以往求天下之安哉？於是合吾分封之臣，而進之於文王之廟，敷其德之在人而可懷思者，以賚爾在位之諸侯；布其功之在人而可慨念者，以封爾有功之臣子。夫豈有他哉？盖欲諸臣各以文王之心爲心，而於斯民之未安者，思有以安之也；皆以文王之德爲德，而於天下之未定者，思有以定之也。如是，則可以副我求定之心，而無愧於

…earnest and sincere, sufficient to move people's hearts. It deeply grasps the intent of the poet and is a fine composition.
Examiner Academician Miao comments: The exposition is thorough and penetrating. The intent of praising righteous virtue [likely a print error for 盛德, abundant virtue] and announcing successful accomplishment shines forth amiably beyond the words themselves.
Examiner Vice Minister Wang comments: Gentle in expression yet full in meaning—this paper has achieved it.

Just as the great enterprise of the former king ought to be received by oneself, the merit and virtue of the former king ought all the more to be spread abroad in order to bring peace to the people. Founding an enterprise is the merit of the former sage, whereas planning for good governance is the responsibility of the later king. Now, when King Wu succeeded to the enterprise of King Wen, if he had not extended King Wen's merit and virtue in order to reward the meritorious, how would he have sought the peace and stability of the realm? This ode praises the achievements of Kings Wen and Wu and speaks of the intent behind the grand enfeoffment of meritorious ministers, as if to say: Our King Wen allowed himself no leisure to eat so as to bring universal harmony to the myriad people, and looked toward the Way as though he had not yet seen it while comforting and possessing the central states; his diligent toil for the world may be called extreme. Now I, his successor, have received and possess it, continuing the great enterprise of holding two-thirds of the realm and inheriting the vast patrimony toward which the four quarters converged. How could I dare to monopolize it for myself and not think of how to go forth and seek the peace of the world? Thereupon he gathered the ministers who were to be enfeoffed and brought them into the temple of King Wen, spreading forth that virtue of his which remained among the people and was worthy of being cherished, so as to reward you feudal lords in office; and proclaiming that merit of his which remained among the people and was worthy of being deeply remembered, so as to enfeoff you meritorious ministers and sons. Was there any other purpose in this? It was simply that he wished all the ministers each to take the heart of King Wen as their own heart, and regarding those among this people who were not yet at peace, to think of how to bring them peace; and all to take the virtue of King Wen as their own virtue, and regarding that part of the world which was not yet settled, to think of how to settle it. If they acted thus, they would fulfill my desire to seek stability, and I would have no cause for shame before…

title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
屢盟而深喜二國之胥命聖人之意爲何如昔者大
道行而天下爲公盟固未之有也周官雖有司盟之
設然邦國有盟必請之天子未聞諸侯可得而私令
入春秋之初我魯隱公首與儀父結好于蔑而私盟
啓矣尋及宋人講成于宿而參盟肇矣未幾齊鄭合
黨于石門而特盟已講宋衞從齊于瓦屋而參盟遂
成前盟甫罷而後盟繼之要言未退而食言已至豈
直王室不得與聞其事哉亦漠乎其無忠信誠愨以
相與矣君子則曰諸侯之屢盟也長亂豈足貴哉故
===
毎書盟者皆不予之也及私盟荐作人習於耳目而
不察其無益於疑怨之釋也於是諸侯講事而不要
結於壇坫之間者鮮矣獨齊衞二君之胥命于蒲也
不然彼以言而諭此此以言而諭彼出由中之信以
相接去刑牲之舉而不疑隱然有古者不盟之風亦
足以矯當時屢盟之弊也君子則曰二國之胥命也
近正有足美也故特起胥命之文以善之嗟乎聖人
之厭屢盟而善胥命意有在矣有虞氏未施信於民
而民信夏后氏未施敬於民而民敬殷人作誓而民始

punctuated: 屢盟，而深喜二國之胥命，聖人之意爲何如？昔者大道行而天下爲公，盟固未之有也。周官雖有司盟之設，然邦國有盟必請之天子，未聞諸侯可得而私令。入春秋之初，我魯隱公首與儀父結好于蔑，而私盟啓矣；尋及宋人講成于宿，而參盟肇矣；未幾，齊、鄭合黨于石門，而特盟已講；宋、衞從齊于瓦屋，而參盟遂成。前盟甫罷而後盟繼之，要言未退而食言已至。豈直王室不得與聞其事哉？亦漠乎其無忠信誠愨以相與矣。君子則曰：「諸侯之屢盟也長亂，豈足貴哉？」故毎書盟者，皆不予之也。及私盟荐作，人習於耳目，而不察其無益於疑怨之釋也，於是諸侯講事而不要結於壇坫之間者鮮矣。獨齊、衞二君之胥命于蒲也不然：彼以言而諭此，此以言而諭彼，出由中之信以相接，去刑牲之舉而不疑，隱然有古者不盟之風，亦足以矯當時屢盟之弊也。君子則曰：「二國之胥命也近正，有足美也。」故特起「胥命」之文以善之。嗟乎！聖人之厭屢盟而善胥命，意有在矣。有虞氏未施信於民而民信，夏后氏未施敬於民而民敬，殷人作誓而民始
translation_en: …frequent covenants, while deeply rejoicing in the mutual pledges of two states—what was the sage's intention? In antiquity, when the Great Way prevailed and all under Heaven was shared in common, covenants certainly did not yet exist. Although the offices of Zhou included the post of Director of Covenants (Simeng), when states made a covenant they had to request permission from the Son of Heaven; it was unheard of for feudal lords to be able to privately command [? make covenants] on their own. At the beginning of the Spring and Autumn period, our Duke Yin of Lu first established friendly relations with Yifu at Mie, and thus private covenants were initiated; shortly thereafter, he negotiated peace with a man of Song at Su, and thus three-party covenants were begun; before long, Qi and Zheng formed a faction at Shimen, and bilateral covenants outside of Lu were already being negotiated; Song and Wei followed Qi at Wawu, and multi-state covenants were thereby established. No sooner had a previous covenant ended than a subsequent covenant followed it; before the binding words had even receded, the breaking of promises had already arrived. Was it merely that the royal house was not allowed to hear of or participate in these affairs? Rather, they were utterly devoid of loyalty, trustworthiness, and sincere honesty in their dealings with one another! The gentleman therefore says: "The frequent covenants of the feudal lords prolong disorder; how could they be worthy of esteem?" Thus, every time a covenant is recorded, it is never with approval. When private covenants repeatedly arose, people grew accustomed to seeing and hearing of them, and failed to realize that they were of no use in dispelling suspicion and resentment. Consequently, when the feudal lords negotiated affairs, it was rare that they did not bind themselves by oaths upon the covenant altar. Only when the two rulers of Qi and Wei made mutual pledges at Pu was it otherwise: the one informed the other through words, and the other informed the one through words; they met one another with trustworthiness coming from within, and dispensed with the act of slaughtering sacrificial victims without harbouring suspicion. In this there faintly remained the ancient custom of not making covenants, which was also sufficient to rectify the contemporary abuse of frequent covenants. The gentleman therefore says: "The mutual pledges of the two states are close to what is proper, and are worthy of praise." Thus, the text specially introduced the phrasing "made mutual pledges" (xuming) in order to commend them. Alas! In the sage's weariness of frequent covenants and his commendation of mutual pledges, there lay a deeper meaning. The Lord of Yu (Shun) had not yet dispensed trustworthiness to the people, yet the people trusted him; the Xia sovereigns had not yet dispensed reverence to the people, yet the people revered them; the people of Yin made oaths, and the people first…

… rebelled; the people of Zhou instituted assemblies and the people began to doubt. That in the end they reached the point of exchanging hostages and still did not trust one another was all the cumulative result of covenants and oaths. That the Sage did not value covenants and instead commended the mutual charge—did he not wish to reform superficiality in favor of good faith, setting his heart upon an age in which all under Heaven is shared in common? Those who study the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) must not fail to explore his intent therein.

The conclusion, which traces back the meaning of the True King and the Hegemon, is especially fine; none who is not well-versed in the teaching of comparing events in the Spring and Autumn Annals could achieve this.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Miao: The two opening statements of this essay are detailed and well-ordered, and its discussion of the Hegemon's achievements and the Sage's transformative influence is clear and worthy of selection.
Comment by Examiner and Vice Minister Wang: The exposition is clear, and the concluding words place the ultimate emphasis upon the Sage; this idea is also good.

When the Hegemon's good faith was made manifest, both barbarians and Chinese were won over in trust; when the Sage's virtue moved the world, both Heaven and man responded in harmony. These were the supreme achievement of Duke Huan of Qi and the marvelous efficacy of the Sage, and both were admirable events in the Spring and Autumn Annals. 小伯之諸夏翕然喻志非信素立何以得此故曰伯

何徴於天哉今鄆讙龜陰之来歸盖齊景以夫子相
===

之不臧而成其好於不偪故歸斯田以謝過焉西狩

punctuated: 於徴貢之師，而待之以退盟之禮，綏之以同好之言，完遂欣然以為其國之福、其君之願，相與歃血而不疑。葵丘之盟，因宰孔言還，而昭大禁以尊王，讀載書以示意，諸侯安之，故束牲不殺而言歸于好。不勞攻戰，而方城、漢水之遠夷帖然聽盟；不待牲歃，而大侯、小伯之諸夏翕然喻志。非信素立，何以得此？故曰：伯信著而夷夏皆孚也。若夫德者，感動天人之本也。夫子温、良、恭、儉、讓，固足以動人矣；而鳳鳥、河圖之有嘆，尚何徴於天哉？今鄆、讙、龜陰之来歸，盖齊景以夫子相禮夾谷，言皆禮義之經，動循古人之道，足以破其謀之不臧，而成其好於不偪，故歸斯田以謝過焉。西狩獲麟，盖由夫子假魯史脩《春秋》，公是非於予奪之際，明典禮於筆削之間，百王之大法斯存，萬世之彜訓由著；文成道備，上動乎天，而麟至焉。片言出，而強國所利之侵疆復入我魯之北鄙；一經成，而聖王所瑞之仁獸倏至我魯之西郊。非德所召，何以臻兹？故曰：聖德感而天人交應也。大抵不即召陵、葵丘之盟，無以知齊桓之功高；不即歸田、獲麟之事，無以驗聖人

…before the army that had come to demand tribute, and treated him with the ritual of withdrawing to make a covenant, reassuring him with words of shared amity, Qu Wan thereupon gladly regarded this as the good fortune of his state and the wish of his ruler, and they smeared their lips with blood together without suspicion. At the covenant of Kuiqiu, because Zai Kong spoke of returning, [Duke Huan] proclaimed the great prohibitions to honor the King and read the covenant document to make known his intent. The feudal lords were set at ease by this, and so they bound the sacrificial victim without slaughtering it and declared their return to friendly relations. Without the toil of attack and battle, the distant barbarians of Fangcheng and the Han River submissively heeded the covenant; without waiting to slaughter the victim and smear blood, the Chinese states of great marquises and lesser earls harmoniously understood his will. Had trustworthiness not been established beforehand, how could this have been achieved? Therefore it is said: the hegemon's trustworthiness was manifest, and both barbarians and Chinese were won over.

As for virtue, it is the foundation for moving Heaven and man. The Master's gentleness, goodness, respectfulness, frugality, and deference were indeed sufficient to move men; yet since he sighed over the phoenix and the River Chart, what verification was there yet from Heaven? Now, the return of the lands of Yun, Huan, and Guiyin came about because Duke Jing of Qi saw that in assisting with the rituals at Jiagu, the Master's words were all the constant principles of ritual propriety and righteousness, and his actions followed the way of the ancients—sufficient to foil their ignoble plot and accomplish friendly relations without coercion; therefore he returned these fields to apologize for his fault. The capture of the unicorn during the western hunt came about because the Master borrowed the history of Lu to compile the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), rendering impartial judgments of right and wrong in his granting and withholding of praise, and clarifying institutional rituals through his writing and deleting. The great laws of the hundred kings were thereby preserved, and the constant lessons for ten thousand generations were thereby made manifest; when the text was completed and the Way fully set forth, it moved Heaven above, and the unicorn arrived. When a single word was uttered, the encroached territories coveted by a powerful state re-entered the northern borders of our state of Lu; when a single classic was completed, the benevolent beast that serves as an auspicious omen for sage kings suddenly arrived in the western suburbs of our state of Lu. Had this not been summoned by virtue, how could such a result have been reached? Therefore it is said: the sage's virtue moved them, and both Heaven and man responded in turn.

…the flourishing of [the Sage's] virtue. Among the deeds of the two hundred and forty-two years of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), none was more glorious than these. Even so, Duke Huan, as a hegemon, merely borrowed the name of benevolence and righteousness to fulfill his desires for profit; how could he compare to the Sage, who personally embodied the Kingly Way—going forth into service to be of benefit to a state, and retiring to compile the Classic so as to serve as a model for posterity? Viewing this, the root and branch of the Kingly Way and the Way of the Hegemon may also be seen in broad outline.

Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Peng comments: In the examination hall, extremely few wrote on this topic, and even among those who occasionally did, none was to the point. Only this essay is clear in principle and rich in style; it ought to be placed among the selected.

Examiner Academician (xueshi) Miao comments: Other essays on this topic mostly erred by being verbose and redundant; only this essay is concise, clear, and worthy of selection.

Examiner Vice Minister (shilang) Wang comments: Those who wrote on this topic mostly missed the original purport; this composition has grasped it.

When a minister serves his ruler, he must join with others to expound and practice the ruler's commands, and he must deliberate upon affairs according to whichever place he is in. For expounding, practicing, and deliberating are what naturally belong to a minister's duty. If one were to expound and practice the ruler's commands without deliberating upon his affairs according to the place, how could that be the way of a minister? Now, he who is the ruler of men dwells in the deep recesses of the Ninefold Palace, whence his edicts and commands issue forth; he occupies the exalted Fifth Position…

punctuated:
惟法令之是降也。為之大夫者，夙夜在公，以行君政，豈不思曰：「王言如絲，其出如綸，可不講明之乎？」為之士者，夙夜匪懈，以敬君事，豈不慮曰：「王言如綸，其出如綍，可不肄習之乎？」於是相與講明之而不敢慢，肄習之而不敢怠焉。然豈但肄習其命而已？必也隨其所在而謀議其事焉。蓋官者，職守司存之處也；人臣在官，則必謀議在官之事，惟恐職掌之不脩。府者，貨器藏貯之所也；人臣在府，則必謀議在府之事，惟慮典守之或闕。庫則府藏之別號，而朝則君臣會見之公庭也；人臣之在庫、在朝，又豈可不謀議所事，以思各盡其職哉？記《禮》君子舉此以明人臣事君之義，至矣。大抵先時豫慮，思不出其位，皆所以虔君命也。虔君命而守其職，以不侵他事、存他慮，則志無所分，政無不舉矣。人臣之道，豈不盡乎？

制度在禮，文為在禮，行之其在人乎？
尹禮
同考試官教諭彭批：論禮之行在人甚詳，而詞且不冗，可以取中。
translation_en:
… sends down only laws and ordinances. Those who serve him as grand masters (dafu) are at their public duties from dawn to night to carry out the ruler's governance; how could they not reflect: "The king's words are like silk threads, yet when they go forth they are like cords—how can we not expound and clarify them?" Those who serve him as servicemen (shi) are untiring from dawn to night in reverently attending to the ruler's affairs; how could they not consider: "The king's words are like cords, yet when they go forth they are like ropes—how can we not practice and master them?" Thereupon they expound and clarify them together without daring to be negligent, and practice and master them without daring to be remiss. Yet how could they merely practice and master his commands and nothing more? Necessarily, wherever they are situated, they deliberate upon the affairs proper to that place. For the office (guan) is where official duties and responsibilities reside; when a minister is at his office, he must deliberate upon the affairs of the office, fearing only that his official charges may not be properly cultivated. The treasury (fu) is where goods and vessels are stored; when a minister is at the treasury, he must deliberate upon the affairs of the treasury, anxious only that his custodial duties might suffer some deficiency. The storehouse (ku) is another name for a repository, while the court (chao) is the public courtyard where ruler and ministers meet in audience; when a minister is at the storehouse or at court, how could he fail to deliberate upon the affairs at hand, thinking of how each may fulfill his own office? That the gentleman who recorded the Record of Rites (Liji) cited these examples to elucidate the principle of how a minister serves his ruler is consummate indeed. On the whole, taking forethought beforehand and not letting one's thoughts go beyond one's position are both means of reverently upholding the ruler's commands. When one reverently upholds the ruler's commands and guards one's office, neither encroaching upon other affairs nor harboring other concerns, one's resolve is undivided and no measure of governance fails to be carried out. Is the Way of the minister not thus fulfilled?

統乎法者在於禮，行乎禮者在於人。盖制度、文為，禮之法也。法固在於禮，行是禮者，又豈不在於人乎？且夫簠簋、爼豆皆制度也，宫室、器皿亦制度也，而設之有等級，制之有次序，何莫而不在於禮焉？升降、上下皆文為也，威儀、進退亦文為也，然行之有節文，施之有隆殺，又何莫而不在於禮焉？盖制度、文為在於禮，皆為禮之法也。然徒法不能以自行，而行之尤在乎人也。苟得夫忠信之人，躬行而實踐之，則制度之在禮者，秩然見於施設之際，而有容之可觀；不然，則制度雖存，徒為虚器耳。文為之在禮者，藹然形諸動作之間，而有儀之可覩；不然，則文為雖施，徒為虚文耳。是禮之行也，必以得人為貴也。豈非統乎法者在於禮，行乎禮者在於人歟？抑論之：制度，體也；文為，用也。二者之於禮也，可相有而不可相無，然行之者則有賴於人也。不然，《禮器》何以曰「無本不立，無文不行」？《中庸》曰「禮儀三百，威儀三千，待其人而後行」？以此觀之，益信。

That which encompasses the regulations lies in ritual, and that which puts ritual into practice lies in people. Indeed, institutional systems and refined enactments are the regulations of ritual. While the regulations inherently reside in ritual, does not putting this ritual into practice reside in people? Now, grain vessels (fu and gui), meat stands (zu), and stemmed bowls (dou) are all institutional systems; palaces, chambers, and utensils are also institutional systems. Yet in setting them up there are gradations of rank, and in regulating them there is proper sequence—how could any of these not reside in ritual? Ascending and descending, going up and going down are all refined enactments; dignified bearing in advancing and withdrawing are also refined enactments. Yet in practicing them there is measured form, and in applying them there are degrees of elevation and diminution—how could any of these not reside in ritual? Indeed, that institutional systems and refined enactments reside in ritual is because they are all the regulations of ritual. However, mere regulations cannot put themselves into practice; putting them into practice depends above all on people. If one obtains men of loyalty and trustworthiness to personally practice and genuinely carry them out, then the institutional systems that reside in ritual will be orderly and manifest when deployed, presenting a deportment worthy of observation; otherwise, even though the institutional systems exist, they are merely empty vessels. The refined enactments that reside in ritual will harmoniously take form amid movements and actions, presenting a ceremony worthy of witnessing; otherwise, even though the refined enactments are applied, they are merely empty forms. Thus, for ritual to be practiced, obtaining the right people must be prized. Is it not the case that what encompasses the regulations lies in ritual, and what puts ritual into practice lies in people? Furthermore, if we discuss it: institutional systems are the substance, while refined enactments are the function. In relation to ritual, the two must coexist and cannot be without one another, yet putting them into practice depends on people. Otherwise, why would the Ritual Vessels (Liqi) chapter say, "Without the root it cannot stand; without refinement it cannot be practiced"? And why does the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) say, "The three hundred rules of ceremony and three thousand rules of demeanor await the right people before they can be put into practice"? Viewed in this light, it is all the more credible.

"Humaneness Encompasses All Goodness in the World"
Yao Long 姚龍
Associate Examiner and Expositor-in-waiting Liu comments: "This discourse traces the fundamental Way of humaneness in the utmost detail; it is no casually dashed-off piece and is well worthy of selection."
Examiner and Academician Miao comments: "It elucidates the greatness of the Way of humaneness, leaving nothing unexpressed."

Great indeed is the Way of humaneness! It encompasses Heaven and Earth, runs through human beings and all things, and cannot be named as merely a single virtue. Although the desirable principles in the world are exceedingly numerous, humaneness is the convergence of those principles; although the admirable virtues in the world are not limited to a single aspect, humaneness is the totality of those virtues. What goodness, then, is not encompassed by humaneness? Anything not encompassed by humaneness cannot be called good. What, in truth, is the nature of humaneness? Heaven and Earth take giving life to things as their mind, and when human beings obtain the life-giving mind of Heaven and Earth as their own mind, that is humaneness. This humaneness, in Heaven, is origination (yuan); among the seasons, it is spring. Heaven has four virtues, and the one that presides over initiating things is origination. Flourishing (heng) is the growth of origination, advantage (li) is the fulfillment of origination, and firmness (zhen) is the completion of origination. Thus, what encompasses the four virtues lies in origination, and extending to the utmost—to the operation of the myriad transformations—there is none that is not encompassed by origination. Time has four seasonal sequences, and the one whose achievement is giving life to things is spring. Summer is the growth of spring, autumn is the harvesting of spring, and winter is the storing of spring. Thus, what encompasses the four seasonal sequences lies in spring, and extending to the utmost—to the ceaseless generation of the myriad categories of beings—there is none that is not encompassed by spring. Humaneness…

translation_en: … resides in human beings is precisely what Origin (yuan) is in Heaven and what spring is in the seasons. For human nature consists of five virtues, all complete within the mind, yet benevolence (ren) alone is the complete virtue of the mind. Righteousness is the regulation of benevolence; propriety is the order of benevolence; wisdom is the discernment of benevolence; and trustworthiness is the substance of benevolence. Benevolence is surely the unifier of the five virtues of human nature! Benevolence unifies the five virtues within this mind, seamlessly whole as though requiring no deliberate effort. Yet when it issues forth from this mind as commiseration, shame and dislike, deference and compliance, and approval and disapproval, these are called the Four Beginnings; when it extends into the Way of father and son, ruler and minister, elder and younger, husband and wife, and friend and friend, these are called the Five Constant Relationships; and when it is stirred into joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate, and desire, these are called the Seven Emotions. Whether the Four Beginnings, the Five Constant Relationships, or the Seven Emotions attaining their proper measure, extending to the appropriateness of the hundred conducts, the conformity to principle of the myriad affairs, and that in which tens of millions of people concur—which of these is not good? And all are unified in benevolence. The reason benevolence can unify all the good under Heaven is that all minds under Heaven are the same; and the reason all minds are the same is that their principle is the same. Since the principle of all under Heaven is the same, how could the good of all under Heaven lie outside of benevolence? The Way of benevolence is truly so great that nothing can be added to it. When Master Zhang of Hengqu [Zhang Zai 張載] composed the book Correcting Youthful Ignorance (Zhengmeng), he spoke to this effect; he may truly be said to have articulated what the former sages had not yet articulated, thereby illuminating how great the Way of benevolence is. Even so, although the greatness of the Way of benevolence certainly leaves not a single good ununified, causing this mind to be lustrous and free of selfish entanglement, vast and utterly impartial, so as to fulfill the capacity of this benevolence and regard all under Heaven with the same benevolence—that depends on the person. Therefore, he whose benevolence was like Heaven was Yao; he who took the love of life as his virtue was Shun. Yao and Shun led all under Heaven with benevolence, and the people followed them. He who was able to achieve benevolence was Tang; he who rested in benevolence was King Wen. Tang and King Wen brought peace to all under Heaven with benevolence, and the people turned to them in allegiance. Why was this? …

…parents, He is purely sincere and purely reverent; He widely seeks out worthy and talented men to appoint to office, and grandly bestows benevolent grace that extends to all creatures. The hundred southern barbarian tribes submit in allegiance, and the myriad states are all at peace. This summons the harmonious ether between Heaven and Earth and manifests auspicious clouds of five colors. Brilliantly spreading like brocade and damask, luminously clear like pearls and gems, they possess the full hues of crimson phoenixes and kingfisher-green simurghs, adding to the splendor of the Golden Gate and Jade Palace. Following the Dragon, they rise high near the Purple Forbidden Enclosure; cradling the Sun, they directly approach the Imperial Canopy. All these are the radiant fulfillment of Sacred Virtue, and truly serve as auspicious responses of Great Peace. Your servants, born in an enlightened era, have been privileged to behold this supreme omen. As we perform the grand ceremonial at the New Year's court audience, we exhaust our humble hearts in offering prayers and praise. With the three blessings of the border warden of Hua, we sing of the Nine Merits of a flourishing age; may Heaven and Earth endure forever, matching the ten-thousand-year longevity of the Sage. Your servants are overcome with the utmost emotion and trepidation as we gaze up at Heaven and look up to the Sage.

Since antiquity, when sage rulers governed All under Heaven, they necessarily had words of instruction and proclamation for their officials and people. When applied to affairs, these could bring about the flourishing of governance and education; when recorded in the Classics, they could hand down lessons for ten thousand generations. Such were King Wu's harangues to his armies and King Cheng's instructions guiding the hundred officials. Coming down to the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, as for the means by which heroic rulers and righteous sovereigns encouraged and exhorted their officials and people—such as the promulgation of edicts and ordinances—their words were far from few. Reaching our own dynasty, this has become especially flourishing. Humbly reflecting on how Emperor Taizu the Exalted displayed his divine martial prowess to first found the realm, and how Emperor Taizong the Cultured broadly spread his great virtue to restore and revitalize the state: sage succeeded sage, tirelessly striving for good governance, and their consideration for their officials and people was far-reaching indeed. In moments of leisure from the myriad affairs of state, they composed the three parts of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao), as well as the two books Secret Blessings for Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi) and True Exemplars of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi), in order to exhort people to exhaust their loyalty, encourage people to do good, and teach people to be filial. Harmonious and mild are these words of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and filial piety! In the prefaces, it is said, "maintain one's heart and uphold one's integrity"; it is said, "spread virtue and bestow kindness"; and it is said, "among the constant principles of Heaven and the righteous ways of Earth, none is more revered than one's parents." text:

恩至渥也為臣民者誠能於三書是訓是行於事君也必
思所以持心操節則能忠矣於治民也必思所以敷

… the Way of a subject, arouse a heart that loves virtue, and all return to a grand and level age of peace—such grace is most abundant indeed. If those who are subjects and commoners can truly take these three books as their instruction and put them into practice: in serving their ruler, they will surely reflect on how to maintain their minds and uphold their integrity, and thus be able to be loyal; in governing the people, they will surely reflect on how to spread virtue and bestow kindness, and thus be able to be benevolent; in serving their parents, they will surely reflect on how to be devoted to the Way of a son, and thus be able to be filial. The Way of cultivating the self truly does not lie outside these three maxims. Yet as for how to practice them throughout one's entire life, how could there not be an essential principle? It is sincerity and nothing more. Sincerity means being true, real, and free of falsehood. Only through sincerity can one firm up one's resolve and ponder deeply, investigating the principles until one attains them; if one does not act with sincerity, it is merely falsehood, and being loyal, being filial, and doing good will all lack reality. This is what subjects and sons ought to clasp to their bosoms and never forget. Therefore it is said: "The gentleman prizes attaining sincerity." I venture to offer this in reply to Your bright inquiry. My humble and narrow view may or may not be correct; I only pray that I may be advanced and instructed.

text:
在天而在聖人聖人之道觀於經可知矣粤自伏羲
因河圖之出畫八卦以發天地之秘此易之所以作
也典謨訓誥載二帝三王治天下之大經大法此書
之所以作也詩則聖人所刪定春秋則聖人所筆削
一以示勸懲一以定褒貶此詩與春秋之所作也聖
人作經之意如此宋邵子謂聖人以經法天者蓋明
夫作經之義也其曰天有四府聖人亦有四府者何
哉春為生物之府夏為長物之府收物之府為秋而
藏物之府為冬也非天之四府乎三皇之時渾渾也
===
如春之生育萬物故以易為生民之府五帝之時明
明也如夏之長茂萬物故書為長民之府三王之時
赫赫也如秋之萬物有成故詩為收民之府五伯非
明明赫赫之時如冬之萬物皆斂矣故以春秋為藏
民之府也非聖人之四府乎天之四時聖人以皇與
帝王伯者配之非所謂法天也歟邵子明作經之意
蓋如此然未止此也繼之曰三皇化民以道五帝教
民以德三王勸民以功五伯率民以力蓋道也德也
功也萬世之所尊而伯者不可與並故以四時之冬

translation_en:
… reside in Heaven, but resides in the sages. The Way of the sages can be known by examining the Classics. Ever since Fuxi, prompted by the emergence of the River Chart (Hetu), drew the Eight Trigrams to reveal the mysteries of Heaven and Earth, this was why the Book of Changes (Yi) was created. The canons, counsels, instructions, and announcements record the great norms and great laws by which the Two Emperors and Three Kings governed the world; this was why the Book of Documents (Shu) was created. The Book of Odes (Shi) was edited and fixed by the sage, and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) was written and pared down by the sage—the one to demonstrate encouragement and warning, the other to establish praise and blame; this was why the Book of Odes and the Spring and Autumn Annals were created. Such was the intention of the sages in creating the Classics.

When Master Shao [Shao Yong] of the Song dynasty said that "the sages modeled themselves on Heaven through the Classics," he was elucidating the meaning of creating the Classics. When he said, "Heaven has four storehouses, and the sages also have four storehouses," what did he mean? Spring is the storehouse for generating things, summer is the storehouse for nurturing things, the storehouse for harvesting things is autumn, and the storehouse for storing things away is winter—are these not the four storehouses of Heaven? The era of the Three Sovereigns was undifferentiated and whole, like spring giving birth to and nurturing the myriad things; therefore the Book of Changes is taken as the storehouse for generating the people. The era of the Five Emperors was bright and illustrious, like summer fostering the lush growth of the myriad things; therefore the Book of Documents is the storehouse for nurturing the people. The era of the Three Kings was glorious and resplendent, like autumn bringing the myriad things to maturity; therefore the Book of Odes is the storehouse for harvesting the people. The era of the Five Hegemons was neither bright and illustrious nor glorious and resplendent, like winter when the myriad things have all withdrawn and contracted; therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals is taken as the storehouse for storing the people away—are these not the four storehouses of the sages? By matching the four seasons of Heaven with the Sovereigns, Emperors, Kings, and Hegemons, is this not what is meant by modeling on Heaven?

Such was how Master Shao elucidated the intention behind creating the Classics. Yet he did not stop here, continuing by saying: "The Three Sovereigns transformed the people through the Way; the Five Emperors taught the people through Virtue; the Three Kings encouraged the people through Merit; the Five Hegemons led the people through Force." For the Way, Virtue, and Merit are what ten thousand generations revere, whereas the Hegemons cannot be placed alongside them; therefore, with winter among the four seasons…

title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
配焉此經之微意非邵子孰能推明至於此哉愚見
如是惟執事幸有以教之
第三問
姚夔
同考試官侍講劉批五策随問随答皆事實不遺筆力
雄健此篇尤詳悉温雅結尤念論春闈得人於此可見
考試官學士苗批此策答者多脫畧而此卷能歷舉
其人以對盖嘗用心于策塲者矣
考試官侍郎王批詳贍非他卷所及前塲既佳尤
===
宜中選
事君當以進賢為務薦賢當以至公為心盖賢才進
則國家得人以為用公道立則賢者以類而登庸人
臣事君非公於薦賢何以哉故周書有曰舉能其官
惟爾之能是人君以舉賢勉其臣也孔子曰舉爾所
知是聖人以舉賢教其弟子也事君而不以舉賢為
務可乎在昔祁奚舉其子午而人不非其舉不避親

title: 正統七年會試錄
text:
要得人蕭望之以經術精通薦薛廣德而講讀得人
練習法令如袁盎之薦張釋之而天下無寃民善聽
獄訟如丙吉之薦于定國而民自不寃此漢臣薦舉
之公也張說之薦張九齡則以其學問該博蕭嵩之
薦韓休則以其行誼純固是非唐臣薦舉之公乎曹
彬名將也教子登壇韜畧世授卒以其子瑋薦呂蒙
正賢相也家法相傳勳業無愧卒以猶子夷簡薦呂
文靖之薦包拯也以其同巷不求見司馬公之薦劉
器之也以其無書抵政府宋臣之公於薦賢也如此
===
盖當時為舉主者皆忠君愛國之良臣而舉必以賢
所舉者皆秉德守正之君子而進必以道故皆赫乎
勳業著於當時昭乎聲光垂於後世誠足以為薦舉
之準的也洪惟
聖人在上屢詔大臣各舉所知不舉者有蔽賢之責謬舉
者有同坐之令意甚盛矣而所舉猶未盡得其人者
無他焉舉主未盡得其人故爾夫人之賢否各以類
從廉謹者舉清介污墨者舉鄙濁其情則然也今欲
所舉盡如古人之可稱則莫若慎擇舉主使不肖者

要得人；蕭望之以經術精通薦薛廣德，而講讀得人；練習法令如袁盎之薦張釋之，而天下無寃民；善聽獄訟如丙吉之薦于定國，而民自不寃：此漢臣薦舉之公也。張說之薦張九齡，則以其學問該博；蕭嵩之薦韓休，則以其行誼純固：是非唐臣薦舉之公乎？曹彬，名將也，教子登壇，韜畧世授，卒以其子瑋薦；呂蒙正，賢相也，家法相傳，勳業無愧，卒以猶子夷簡薦；呂文靖之薦包拯也，以其同巷不求見；司馬公之薦劉器之也，以其無書抵政府：宋臣之公於薦賢也如此。
盖當時為舉主者，皆忠君愛國之良臣，而舉必以賢；所舉者，皆秉德守正之君子，而進必以道。故皆赫乎勳業著於當時，昭乎聲光垂於後世，誠足以為薦舉之準的也。洪惟聖人在上，屢詔大臣各舉所知，不舉者有蔽賢之責，謬舉者有同坐之令，意甚盛矣。而所舉猶未盡得其人者，無他焉，舉主未盡得其人故爾。夫人之賢否，各以類從：廉謹者舉清介，污墨者舉鄙濁，其情則然也。今欲所舉盡如古人之可稱，則莫若慎擇舉主，使不肖者

…pivotal positions [?] gained the right man; Xiao Wangzhi 蕭望之 recommended Xue Guangde 薛廣德 for his mastery of classical learning, and imperial lecturing and reading gained the right man; for familiarity with laws and ordinances, there was Yuan Ang's 袁盎 recommendation of Zhang Shizhi 張釋之, so that there were no wronged commoners in the realm; and for skill in hearing litigation, there was Bing Ji's 丙吉 recommendation of Yu Dingguo 于定國, so that the people felt no grievance of their own accord. Such was the impartiality of Han ministers in making recommendations. Zhang Yue 張說 recommended Zhang Jiuling 張九齡 for the breadth of his learning, and Xiao Song 蕭嵩 recommended Han Xiu 韓休 for the purity and firmness of his conduct and principles—was this not the impartiality of Tang ministers in making recommendations? Cao Bin 曹彬 was a renowned general; he taught his sons to ascend the commander's dais, passing down military strategy through the generations, and ultimately recommended his own son Cao Wei 曹瑋. Lü Mengzheng 呂蒙正 was a worthy grand councilor; his family traditions were handed down and his meritorious achievements were beyond reproach, and he ultimately recommended his nephew Lü Yijian 呂夷簡. When Lü Wenjing 呂文靖 (Lü Yijian) recommended Bao Zheng 包拯, it was because although they lived in the same lane, Bao never sought an audience with him; when Lord Sima 司馬公 (Sima Guang 司馬光) recommended Liu Qizhi 劉器之 (Liu Anshi 劉安世), it was because Liu never sent letters to the Administration Chamber. Such was the impartiality of Song ministers in recommending the worthy.

Indeed, those who served as sponsors at the time were all good ministers loyal to their ruler and devoted to the state, and they invariably recommended on the basis of worthiness; those whom they recommended were all noble men who upheld virtue and maintained rectitude, and they invariably advanced in accordance with the Way. Therefore, their illustrious achievements were manifest in their own time, and their bright reputations were handed down to later generations; truly, they suffice to serve as the standard for recommendations. Humbly reflecting on how the Sage is on the throne above and has repeatedly decreed that the grand ministers should each recommend those whom they know—with reprimands for concealing the worthy if they fail to recommend, and ordinances for joint liability if they recommend erroneously—His intention is magnificent indeed! Yet if those who are recommended are still not all the right men, there is no other reason for it than that the sponsors themselves are not all the right men. Whether men are worthy or unworthy, each follows his own kind: the incorrupt and prudent recommend the pure and upright, while the venal and corrupt recommend the base and turbid—such is the nature of things. □□，然歷代所選之得人，與所教之法，亦□□□也。自成周簡教之法廢，於是漢有良家子、六郡射、募騎士、立功之選。若李廣戰輒有功，屢却單于；趙充國圖上方畧，坐困西羌；他如公孫賀、傅介子、甘延壽之徒，亦皆當時名將，率有軍功，則漢之武舉得人可知矣。唐武舉有長垛、馬射、步射、馬鎗、翹關、負重、身材之選，天寶間復置明孫吳兵法之科，裴端復、郭子儀皆從此而出。裴之功業未著，而子儀再造唐室，功盖天下，則唐之武舉得人可見矣。宋開寶間有文經武緯之舉，天聖間復沿唐制置軍謀武藝之科，高志寧、令狐挺亦皆從此而出。志寧以元昊之必叛，其言果然，韓琦以其料敵比淮陰；挺教狄青擣儂智高之虛，畢仲游謂其能籌度萬里。宋武舉以二人為最，他如馬隆以編廂制勝，韓世忠以兵破金人，宋武舉之得人如此。
